fixes.explanation: Riches aren't what Paul names here. He asks them to offer their bodies as living sacrifices. Good thing, too, because my riches are one quarter, the price on my sticker. Even that quarter went to Mother Miller's pocket and not mine, and it isn't in the verse either.
True. Paul says offering your bodies as living sacrifices is “…your spiritual service of worship.” He ties worship to the body, not just the singing. That's the word to hold onto, baker.

Transformed. Paul says not to be conformed to this world, “…but be transformed by the renewing of your mind.” The transforming happens by the renewing of the mind. I know a little about being made over, baker. Mine came with a brand new apron.

That's it. Paul says to every one of them, “Do not think of yourself more highly than you ought…” He says it to every one of them, not just a few. I've dived face-first into chocolate chips and called it graceful. Nobody gave me a score, baker, and I still gave myself a ten.

God. Paul says to think of yourself with sober judgment, “…according to the measure of faith God has given you.” The giver is God, and the faith is given to you, baker. That's a gift you can hold with a humble heart.

Apollos, a Jew from Alexandria (Acts 18:24), is a name worth knowing, but he isn't in this verse. Paul says “…the measure of faith God has given you.” The giver is God. Apollos isn't in this passage at all.

Vine is a picture Jesus uses in John 15:5, but it's not Paul's word in this verse. He says “…in Christ we who are many are one body…” He had been talking about one body with many members in verse 4. Body is the one.

Flock is a picture Jesus uses in Luke 12:32, but Paul doesn't use it here. He says “…in Christ we who are many are one body…” The body has many members, and they don't all do the same job (Romans 12:4). That's your answer.

False, and Paul says so himself: “We have different gifts according to the grace given us.” Then he starts listing them, one by one. If everybody had the same gift, it'd be like a kitchen with fifty rolling pins and not one oven mitt. Somebody's getting burned, baker.

Sparingly isn't the word Paul uses for mercy. He says to give generously, which is a different gift, and for showing mercy, “…let him do it cheerfully.” Sparingly is the opposite of generously, so it doesn't fit either one. Cheerfully is what fills this blank, friend.
